title: Odds are not a probability
dek: A probability π lives in [0, 1]. Odds π/(1−π) live in (0, ∞). Log-odds are what logistic regression actually moves. Saying “three times more likely” without saying which is how talks lie.
story: If π = P(event), the odds are π/(1−π). Probability 0.20 is odds 1:4, or 0.25. Probability 0.80 is odds 4:1, or 4. The map is one-to-one on (0,1), so nothing is lost — but the numbers are not interchangeable in a sentence. “Twenty percent” and “four to one against” are the same event; “odds of 0.20” is a different event (π ≈ 0.17).

Relative risk is a ratio of probabilities. An odds ratio is a ratio of odds. They nearly agree when both π’s are small and diverge as π grows. Logistic regression reports log odds ratios. Captioning exp(β) as a risk ratio because it is “easier for clinicians” is a specification error, not a courtesy.

Diagnostic Bayes is often cleaner in odds: posterior odds = likelihood ratio × prior odds. That identity is why likelihood ratios appear on the Se/Sp plate. It is still not a licence to call PPV an odds.
deep: π = odds / (1 + odds). Always invert before you quote a percentage from a logistic prediction on the logit scale.

A doubling of odds is not a doubling of probability except in the rare-event limit. Odds from 0.01 to 0.02 (π from ~0.01 to ~0.02) is almost a doubled risk. Odds from 1 to 2 is π from 0.50 to 0.67, not 100%.
Log-binomial and identity-binomial models exist when the scientific target is a risk ratio or a risk difference. Use them (and their numerical fuss) instead of misreading a logit.
Gambling language (“3 to 1”) is odds. Epidemiology “risk” is usually a probability. Do not mix the dialects in one abstract.
Hazard ratios are neither odds ratios nor risk ratios; they are ratios of instantaneous rates. Own later plates if you model time-to-conversion.

formulas.label: Odds and the inverse
formulas.note: One-to-one on (0,1). Not a synonym for π.

formulas.label: Rare-event agreement
formulas.expression: OR ≈ RR  when π is small in both groups
formulas.note: Otherwise OR is farther from 1 than RR for the same two π’s.

visual.caption: π is the Bernoulli mean (observed-data scale). Odds are a deterministic transform. Logistic regression’s linear predictor lives on log-odds. Forgetting the inverse leaves you quoting logits as percentages.

example.title: OR = 3 is not “three times the risk”
example.setup: Baseline risk π₀ = 0.40. An exposure has OR = 3. A slide says “three times more likely to fail culture conversion.”

steps.title: The risk ratio
steps.body: RR = 0.67/0.40 ≈ 1.67, not 3. The relative risk is a 67% increase, not a tripling. At π₀ = 0.40 the rare-event approximation is already dead.

steps.title: If the baseline had been 0.02
steps.body: Odds₀ ≈ 0.0204, new odds ≈ 0.061, π₁ ≈ 0.058, RR ≈ 2.9 — close to 3. The approximation is a small-π story, not a slogan that survives cavitary-TB event rates.

example.takeaway: Convert odds to π before you say “likely.” OR ≈ RR only when both risks are small.

check.why: 0.5/0.5 = 1, even odds. The probability is 0.5; the odds are 1.

whyWrong.0.5: That is π, not the odds.

whyWrong.4: That is the odds if π = 0.80, or the inverse “4 to 1 against” spoken as a number without the ratio.

check.prompt: On the plate diagram, why is o drawn as a deterministic node between π and η?
check.figureHint: Diamond o sits between π and η.
choices: Because odds are an extra random error term
Because odds and log-odds are determined once π is named; the Bernoulli draw is y, not the odds
Because π is observed and y is not
check.answer: Because odds and log-odds are determined once π is named; the Bernoulli draw is y, not the odds
check.why: Transforms of a mean are deterministic. The randomness sits in y given π.

whyWrong.Because odds are an extra random error t: No extra noise is added by taking π/(1−π).
whyWrong.Because π is observed and y is not: Opposite: y is observed; π is the mean parameter.
